phases.title: Build the Coalition
phases.scenario: The idea has energy, but a public facility needs trusted people around the table. Choose the first move.
phases.fieldNote: Coleman Bike Park and the Warwick discussions emphasize relationships among park boards, municipalities, builders, riders, families, and community supporters.
phases.guide: Start with people. A track is easier to draw than a coalition is to build—and the coalition is what keeps the project alive.

choices.label: Show up with a coalition
choices.detail: Coordinate riders, families, an experienced builder, and municipal conversations from the beginning.
choices.result: Recognizable supporters and practical experience give decision-makers a reason to keep listening.

choices.label: Launch a public campaign first
choices.detail: Build visible enthusiasm before formal technical planning.
choices.result: Public enthusiasm grows quickly, but the project still needs technical and municipal grounding.

choices.label: Recruit a builder quietly
choices.detail: Develop a credible preliminary concept before broad outreach.
choices.result: The concept becomes more realistic, though fewer residents understand why it matters.

phases.title: Screen the Site
phases.scenario: A promising parcel appears. Decide what the team must establish before treating it as the future home of the track.
phases.fieldNote: Public pump-track planning involves land availability, drainage, utilities, circulation, neighboring uses, parking, and future maintenance—not only the visible riding area.
phases.guide: The empty-looking field is never truly empty. Water, utilities, access, neighbors, and future maintenance are already part of the site.

choices.label: Run a full feasibility screen
choices.detail: Study drainage, utilities, access, parking, neighbors, ownership, and expansion potential together.
choices.result: The project slows briefly but gains a defensible site story and fewer hidden surprises.

choices.label: Prioritize visibility and rail-trail access
choices.detail: Focus first on a visible, connected location that people can reach easily.
choices.result: The public value is easy to see, but utilities and drainage still need deeper review.

choices.label: Choose the easiest available land
choices.detail: Move quickly on the parcel that appears easiest to obtain.
choices.result: Momentum jumps, but unresolved site conditions become a major project risk.

phases.title: Choose the Footprint
phases.scenario: The township asks the question that changes the conversation: “How much land do you need?” Choose a planning footprint.
phases.fieldNote: The Warwick meeting update documented possibilities from roughly 9,000 square feet to more than 43,000 square feet. These are game planning scenarios, not engineering recommendations.
phases.guide: Bigger is not automatically better. Match the footprint to the coalition, site, maintenance plan, and realistic first phase.

choices.label: 9,000 sq ft grassroots pilot
choices.detail: A compact first phase that can prove demand and build experience.
choices.result: The smaller footprint feels achievable, but limits simultaneous uses and future design options.

choices.label: 24,000 sq ft balanced community track
choices.detail: A medium footprint with room for broad use, circulation, and phasing.
choices.result: The project gains space to serve more users without immediately pursuing the largest build.

choices.label: 43,000+ sq ft regional destination
choices.detail: Plan for major growth, events, and long-term regional draw.
choices.result: The vision is exciting, but land, funding, and maintenance demands rise sharply.

phases.title: Select the Build Strategy
phases.scenario: Choose how the first public version of the Warwick Township track will be built.
phases.fieldNote: Pump Track Chat compares dirt, asphalt, concrete, municipal support, private support, and phased development.
phases.guide: The surface changes who can ride, how weather affects the track, what maintenance looks like, and how much funding the first phase needs.

choices.label: Grassroots dirt build
choices.detail: Use volunteer energy and a lower-resource approach with regular maintenance.
choices.result: Progress can become visible quickly, but weather and continuing maintenance become central risks.

choices.label: Phased asphalt plan
choices.detail: Open a practical first phase while preserving a path for later expansion.
choices.result: The project balances durability and ambition while keeping the full vision expandable.

choices.label: Full paved destination build
choices.detail: Pursue the complete durable facility in one major construction phase.
choices.result: Durability and broad use improve, but the funding and approval burden grows immediately.

phases.title: Design for the People Who Will Use It
phases.scenario: The riding surface must serve a real public. Choose the design priority.
phases.fieldNote: Brandon discusses bicycles, scooters, skateboards, families, beginners, and adaptive riders, including the distinction between access to the park and meaningful access to the riding experience.
phases.guide: “Everyone can enter the park” is not the same as “everyone can meaningfully use the facility.” Design access into the experience.

choices.label: All wheels + adaptive access
choices.detail: Plan circulation, transitions, rest areas, and riding opportunities for broad use.
choices.result: The concept serves the broadest public and gains credibility, with added design and funding needs.

choices.label: Competition-first layout
choices.detail: Prioritize speed, progression, and advanced riding features.
choices.result: Experienced riders gain a strong facility, but the public-use case narrows.

choices.label: Beginner and family loop
choices.detail: Prioritize low-pressure entry, visibility, and family use.
choices.result: The project becomes welcoming and understandable, though advanced progression is limited at first.

phases.title: Write the Maintenance Story
phases.scenario: Before the public presentation, someone asks who will care for the track five years after opening.
phases.fieldNote: Construction is only the beginning. Surface choice, drainage, inspections, landscaping, repairs, staffing, volunteer capacity, and operating responsibility shape long-term success.
phases.guide: A project without a maintenance owner is a future closure story. Name the work, the schedule, and the responsible partners now.

choices.label: Shared municipal + partner plan
choices.detail: Define inspections, budget responsibility, volunteer roles, and professional repair needs.
choices.result: The proposal becomes more believable because long-term work has named owners.

choices.label: Volunteer stewardship model
choices.detail: Build a rider-led maintenance group around recurring work days.
choices.result: Community ownership grows, but volunteer availability remains a long-term vulnerability.

choices.label: Address maintenance after approval
choices.detail: Keep the proposal focused on getting the track built first.
choices.result: The pitch moves faster, but decision-makers see an unresolved operating risk.

phases.title: The Rain Test
phases.scenario: Heavy rain exposes ponding near the proposed low section. Choose the response.
phases.fieldNote: This is a fictional setback designed to teach why drainage and access review belong inside pump-track planning.
phases.guide: A setback is information. The question is whether the team uses it to improve the plan or hides it to protect the schedule.

choices.label: Pause for drainage and access review
choices.detail: Recheck grading, runoff, paths, and the relationship between drainage and accessible circulation.
choices.result: The schedule slips, but the project gains technical trust and a safer long-term plan.

choices.label: Redesign the lowest section
choices.detail: Make a targeted correction while preserving the overall concept.
choices.result: The team responds without restarting everything, though broader site questions remain.

choices.label: Keep the schedule
choices.detail: Treat the storm as unusual and continue toward the meeting.
choices.result: The presentation stays on time, but the unresolved problem weakens public trust.

phases.title: Bring the Community Into the Process
phases.scenario: The design is taking shape. Decide how residents, riders, families, and neighbors will experience it before the next formal step.
phases.fieldNote: The documented Warwick effort frames the project as a community and family asset, not simply a set of dirt jumps.
phases.guide: People support what they understand and help shape. Make room for questions, demonstrations, concerns, and new users—not only applause.

choices.label: Ride, roll, and listening day
choices.detail: Combine a demonstration, accessible explanation, neighbor listening, and feedback stations.
choices.result: The public can see the idea, test assumptions, and contribute before the proposal hardens.

choices.label: Formal presentation only
choices.detail: Use one polished meeting to control the message and limit cost.
choices.result: The project appears organized, but fewer people develop ownership in it.

choices.label: Small stakeholder meetings
choices.detail: Meet separately with neighbors, families, cycling groups, and potential partners.
choices.result: Trust grows through focused conversations, though public visibility develops more slowly.

phases.title: Make the Final Pitch
phases.scenario: The next meeting is approaching. Choose the core promise the proposal will make.
phases.fieldNote: The real project remains subject to Warwick Township, professional review, community stakeholders, funding, and formal decisions. The game cannot approve it.
phases.guide: Do not promise a fantasy. Explain who benefits, what the first phase requires, how risks will be managed, and why the project is worth continuing.

choices.label: Phased community-asset plan
choices.detail: Present a durable first phase, broad access, transparent risks, and a path to expansion.
choices.result: The pitch connects ambition to a realistic next step and a clear public-use case.

choices.label: Regional destination and events
choices.detail: Lead with tourism, major events, and long-term regional identity.
choices.result: The vision is memorable, but decision-makers still need a grounded first-phase plan.

choices.label: Fastest low-cost opening
choices.detail: Lead with speed, volunteer energy, and the smallest immediate ask.
choices.result: The proposal feels attainable, but durability, access, and long-term care remain weak.
